result.overall: The appeal is allowed, the Federal Court judgment is set aside, and the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) decision is confirmed because the RAD reasonably interpreted subsection 110(4) of the IRPA and correctly refused to admit the Diploma as new evidence, which was not truly new or unavailable to the respondent.

themes.name: Standard of review for statutory interpretation
themes.summary: The court discusses and confirms that the reasonableness standard applies to the RAD's interpretation of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, with deference owed to the administrative tribunal's expertise.

themes.name: Admissibility criteria for new evidence under subsection 110(4) IRPA
themes.summary: The court analyzes the explicit and implicit criteria for admitting new evidence on appeal, concluding that the criteria from Raza for paragraph 113(a) apply mutatis mutandis to subsection 110(4), with necessary adaptations.

themes.name: Role and function differences between RAD and PRRA officers
themes.summary: The court considers the different roles of the RAD and PRRA officers but finds these differences do not justify a different approach to admissibility criteria for new evidence under subsection 110(4).

themes.name: Responsibility for evidence and counsel's role
themes.summary: The court holds that the respondent must live with the consequences of his counsel's failure to submit evidence and that no complaint or incompetence was established to excuse the respondent's failure to present the Diploma earlier.

themes.name: Charter considerations and procedural fairness
themes.summary: The court rejects the argument that Charter values require a more flexible approach to admitting new evidence, finding no breach of fundamental justice or Charter rights in the RAD's decision to exclude the Diploma.

arguments.quote: The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (the Minister) argued that the Federal Court erred in failing to apply the criteria laid out in Raza v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FCA 385, [2007] F.C.J. No 1632 [Raza] for the purposes of subsection 110(4), and that the RAD was entitled to refuse to admit into evidence a grade 12 diploma (the Diploma) that had been seized by the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) and that had not been submitted before the RPD.
arguments.claim: The Minister argued that the Federal Court erred in not applying the Raza criteria for subsection 110(4) and that the Refugee Appeal Division was entitled to refuse to admit a grade 12 diploma seized by CBSA and not submitted before the Refugee Protection Division.

arguments.quote: First, the RPD found that the respondent had failed to establish his identity. In this regard, it noted that the CBSA had determined that the driver’s licence and voter’s card were probably forgeries, and opined that his credibility had been undermined by the fact that he had not made any efforts to obtain genuine versions of these documents through his family in India.
arguments.claim: The Refugee Protection Division found the respondent failed to establish his identity, noting probable forgery of identity documents and lack of effort to obtain genuine documents.

arguments.quote: As for the school certificates, the RPD’s record contained only the one that had been issued in 2000. Questioned about the 2002 Diploma, the respondent stated that he believed that it was still in the possession of Citizenship and Immigration Canada and that he did not understand why a copy of it had not been forwarded to the RPD. This explanation was rejected by the RPD, and as a result there was no evidence to corroborate his claim of having studied with Bhupinder Singh until 2002.
arguments.claim: The Refugee Protection Division's record contained only the 2000 school certificate; the respondent's explanation for the missing 2002 diploma was rejected, leaving no evidence to corroborate his study claim.

arguments.quote: Lastly, the respondent had produced a copy of a ration card as well as a birth certificate. The ration card had been issued in 2008 but had been corrected in 2011 to remove the respondent’s sister and replace the family photo, following his sister’s marriage in 2010. The RPD found that the one-year gap between the marriage and the correction to the family’s ration card affected the probative value of the document, since the photo attached to the ration card seemed to have been affixed permanently rather than in a manner that would permit it to be changed.
arguments.claim: The respondent produced a ration card and birth certificate; the ration card had been corrected a year after his sister's marriage, affecting its probative value due to the permanent photo attachment.

arguments.quote: Given that the four identity documents filed as evidence by the respondent raised concerns, the birth certificate alone was not sufficient to establish his identity.
arguments.claim: Given concerns with four identity documents, the birth certificate alone was insufficient to establish the respondent's identity.

arguments.quote: Second, the RPD continued its analysis to conclude that the respondent’s narrative was not credible. The RPD pointed out that the respondent had changed the chronology of important events when he amended his Basis of Claim form, having initially placed his father’s cardiac problems after the two arrests, and then between the two arrests. Given the significance of the events in question, the RPD did not accept the respondent’s explanation that he had made a mistake with the dates and had only realized his error when he received his father’s medical report. The RPD also noted that this medical report only indicated facial paralysis and bed rest for a five-day period, which does not correspond to the claim that his father was half paralysed and permanently bedridden. The RPD further concluded that the medical report relating to the respondent’s stomach issues did not corroborate his allegations of torture.
arguments.claim: The RPD found the respondent's narrative not credible due to inconsistencies in the chronology of events and discrepancies in medical reports.

arguments.quote: Even if the respondent had been able to establish his identity and the credibility of his narrative, the RPD ultimately found that he still had an internal flight alternative. While acknowledging that Indian police have the ability to pursue individuals throughout the country, the RPD nonetheless noted that only a limited group of militant Sikhs were targeted in this manner, and that the respondent did not have the profile of someone who would be targeted, were he to move elsewhere in India.
arguments.claim: The RPD found that the respondent had an internal flight alternative despite acknowledging the Indian police's ability to pursue individuals nationwide.

arguments.quote: On appeal at the RAD, the respondent submitted an application to file additional evidence, namely, a copy of the Diploma. In support of his application, he filed an affidavit attesting that he had received from his former counsel, on or about June 11, 2013, a copy of his file that included a copy of the Diploma, which had apparently been faxed to his former counsel by the CBSA on February 25, 2013. He pointed out that he had been unaware of this fact prior to June 11, 2013, that it was consequently impossible for him to have produced the document before the RPD, and that he was therefore justified in asserting during his hearing before the RPD that the Diploma had been seized.
arguments.claim: The respondent applied to the RAD to file additional evidence, specifically a copy of the Diploma, which he claimed he was unaware of before June 11, 2013.

arguments.quote: The RAD refused to allow the Diploma to be admitted into evidence. It first opined that subsection 110(4) of the IRPA should be interpreted in light of the jurisprudence that has developed around paragraph 113(a) of the same statute, and in particular on the basis of Raza, given the similar wording used in both provisions. The RAD also pointed out that the fact that evidence corroborates allegations or contradicts the findings of the RPD does not make it new evidence. Ultimately, the RAD found that the Diploma had been available to the respondent at the time of the hearing on April 2, 2013, since a copy of it had been sent to his former counsel on February 25, 2013. Considering that the respondent had not alleged any incompetence or made a complaint against his former counsel, he and his counsel had access to the Diploma and it was reasonable to expect that the document would have been presented at the hearing before the RPD. Accordingly, the RAD concluded that the Diploma was inadmissible, and as a result, that there was no ground to hold a hearing.
arguments.claim: The RAD refused to admit the Diploma as new evidence, interpreting subsection 110(4) IRPA in light of Raza and finding the Diploma was available before the RPD hearing.

arguments.quote: On the merits, the RAD was of the view that the three issues should be reviewed on a standard of reasonableness. With respect to the identity of the respondent, the RAD concluded that the RPD had erred by failing to make a finding on the probative value of the school certificates to establish the respondent’s identity, analyzing them solely from the perspective of his credibility as to whether he had gone to school with Bhupinder Singh. Therefore, the RPD could not dismiss the birth certificate on the basis that this document alone was insufficient to establish the respondent’s identity. The RAD therefore found that the respondent’s identity had been duly established based on his school certificate and birth certificate. Second, the RAD was of the view that the RPD had not made an error of fact or of law in its overall assessment of the respondent’s credibility, and that it could reasonably doubt his credibility in light of the varying information with regard to the chronology of events he claimed to have experienced, the fraudulent or altered documents he presented as evidence, and the medical documents that did not corroborate his allegations.
arguments.claim: The RAD reviewed the issues on a reasonableness standard and found the respondent's identity established based on school and birth certificates, but upheld the RPD's credibility doubts.

arguments.quote: Given these findings, the RAD was of the opinion that it was not necessary for it to respond to the internal flight alternative issue.
arguments.claim: The RAD considered it unnecessary to address the internal flight alternative issue given its findings on identity and credibility.

arguments.quote: II. The Federal Court judgment [17] Two issues were raised in the application for judicial review before the Federal Court. First the Court had to determine whether the RAD erred in applying the criteria in Raza to assess the admissibility of new evidence, and then consider the application of those criteria to the facts of the case. In both cases, the judge applied the reasonableness standard of review. The first issue concerned the interpretation of the RAD’s home statute and was not subject to any of the exceptions to the presumption that this type of question is reviewable on the reasonableness standard, while the second was clearly a question of mixed fact and law.
arguments.claim: The Federal Court had to determine whether the RAD erred in applying the criteria in Raza for admissibility of new evidence and the application of those criteria to the facts, reviewing both on a reasonableness standard.

arguments.quote: After comparing the wording of subsection 110(4) and paragraph 113(a) of the IRPA and acknowledging that the language was similar, the judge began by noting that the role of a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (PRRA) officer differed from that of the the RAD.
arguments.claim: The judge noted that the role of a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment (PRRA) officer differs from that of the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD).

arguments.quote: While PRRA officers are employees of the Minister and must show deference to decisions made by the RPD unless new evidence arises that would require a re-assessment of the risks set out in sections 96 and 97, the RAD is a quasi-judicial administrative tribunal that has been given the mandate of hearing appeals from decisions issued by the RPD and may set aside a decision in order to substitute the determination that, in its opinion, should have been made (IRPA, s. 111(1)).
arguments.claim: PRRA officers are employees of the Minister and must show deference to decisions made by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) unless new evidence arises, whereas the RAD is a quasi-judicial administrative tribunal that hears appeals from RPD decisions and may substitute its own determination.

arguments.quote: Given these distinctive roles, the judge was of the opinion that it was not appropriate to apply, mutatis mutandis, the criteria developed in the context of paragraph 113(a) to interpret subsection 110(4).
arguments.claim: Given the distinctive roles of PRRA officers and the RAD, the judge found it inappropriate to apply the criteria developed for paragraph 113(a) mutatis mutandis to interpret subsection 110(4).

arguments.quote: Relying on a statement made in the House of Commons by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration during a debate on the establishment of the RAD to the effect that refugee claimants must be able to benefit from a “full fact-based appeal”, the judge continued this line of reasoning by adding that adopting a restrictive approach to the admissibility of new evidence would prevent the RAD from fulfilling its mission.
arguments.claim: The judge relied on a statement by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration that refugee claimants must benefit from a 'full fact-based appeal' to argue that a restrictive approach to admissibility of new evidence would prevent the RAD from fulfilling its mission.

arguments.quote: Lastly, she noted that the implicit factors identified by the Federal Court of Appeal in Raza “find their source in the purpose of paragraph 113(a)”, according to Justice Sharlow herself. That being the case, the judge added, these factors are not transferable in the context of an appeal before the RAD.
arguments.claim: The judge noted that the implicit factors identified by the Federal Court of Appeal in Raza originate from the purpose of paragraph 113(a) and are not transferable to appeals before the RAD under subsection 110(4).

arguments.quote: Having concluded that it was unreasonable for the RAD to have strictly applied the criteria established in Raza when it came time to interpret subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, the judge then inquired as to whether it was reasonable for the tribunal to have refused to admit the Diploma into evidence.
arguments.claim: The judge concluded it was unreasonable for the RAD to strictly apply the criteria from Raza when interpreting subsection 110(4) of the IRPA.

arguments.quote: She determined that this piece of evidence could be material to demonstrate that the RPD erred in making negative findings with respect to the respondent’s credibility, namely, that the CBSA had not confiscated the Diploma and that the respondent had not established that he had attended school with Bhupinder Singh until 2002.
arguments.claim: The judge found that the Diploma evidence could be material to show that the RPD erred in negative credibility findings about the respondent, including that the CBSA had not confiscated the Diploma and that the respondent had not established attending school with Bhupinder Singh until 2002.

arguments.quote: The judge also found it unreasonable for the RAD to have concluded that the respondent should have brought this evidence before the RPD, given that it was not in his possession and that he mistakenly believed that the CBSA still had it.
arguments.claim: The judge found it unreasonable for the RAD to conclude the respondent should have brought the Diploma evidence before the RPD, given it was not in his possession and he mistakenly believed the CBSA still had it.

arguments.quote: As for the fact that the respondent did not file a complaint against his former counsel, the judge opined that it was unreasonable to make this a prerequisite for filing new evidence or to expect the respondent to know the procedure for filing complaints before the Barreau du Québec.
arguments.claim: The judge found it unreasonable to require the respondent to file a complaint against former counsel as a prerequisite for filing new evidence or to expect the respondent to know the complaint procedure before the Barreau du Québec.

arguments.quote: III. Issues [21] The Federal Court judge certified the following two questions: 1. What standard of review should be applied by this Court when reviewing the Refugee Appeal Division’s interpretation of subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27? 2. In considering the role of a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment officer and that of the Refugee Appeal Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board sitting in appeal of a decision of the Refugee Protection Division, does the test set out in Raza v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FCA 385, for the interpretation of paragraph 113(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, LC 2001, c 27, apply to its subsection 110(4)?
arguments.claim: The Federal Court judge certified two questions: (1) the standard of review to be applied when reviewing the RAD's interpretation of subsection 110(4) IRPA; and (2) whether the test set out in Raza for paragraph 113(a) applies to subsection 110(4).

arguments.quote: As noted earlier, the judge applied the reasonableness standard to the interpretation of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA.
arguments.claim: The judge applied the reasonableness standard to the interpretation of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA.

arguments.quote: The intervener nonetheless asserted that the judge erred in selecting a reasonableness standard, on the ground that she had an obligation to put an end to the differences in interpretation resulting from the wording of subsection 110(4) within the RAD.
arguments.claim: The intervener asserted that the judge erred in selecting a reasonableness standard, arguing that she had an obligation to end the differences in interpretation within the RAD regarding subsection 110(4).

arguments.quote: Relying on this Court’s recent decision in Wilson, the intervener related the various different approaches adopted by RAD members in applying subsection 110(4) and requested that we put an end to this uncertainty and to the conflicting results that are likely to result from it.
arguments.claim: The intervener relied on this Court’s recent decision in Wilson to highlight different approaches by RAD members and requested the Court to end the uncertainty and conflicting results.

arguments.quote: That said, there was reason to believe that this Court owed no deference with regard to the decision made by an administrative decision-maker in the context of the IRPA, where the certified question on the basis of which the Federal Court decision was being appealed raised an issue of statutory interpretation.
arguments.claim: The Court owed no deference to the administrative decision-maker's interpretation of the IRPA in the context of a certified question raising statutory interpretation.

arguments.quote: After all, the Federal Court may only certify serious questions of general importance that transcend the interests of the parties: IRPA, s. 79. Is this not precisely the type of question that requires a definitive interpretation and on which the Court of Appeal should rightly intervene to put a stop to inconsistencies that may develop within an administrative body?
arguments.claim: The Federal Court may only certify serious questions of general importance that transcend the parties' interests, warranting definitive interpretation by the Court of Appeal.

arguments.quote: At least, this is what was suggested in decisions such as Hilewitz v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration); De Jong v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2005 SCC 57, [2005] 2 S.C.R. 706 and Pushpanathan v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), [1998] 1 S.C.R. 982, 160 D.L.R. (4th) 193. In that last matter, Justice Bastarache (writing for the majority) states at paragraph 43: First, s. 83(1) would be incoherent if the standard of review were anything other than correctness. The key to the legislative intention as to the standard of review is the use of the words “a serious question of general importance” (emphasis added). The general importance of the question, that is, its applicability to numerous future cases, warrants the review by a court of justice. Would that review serve any purpose if the Court of Appeal were obliged to defer to incorrect decisions of the Board? Is it possible that the legislator would have provided for an exceptional appeal to the Court of Appeal on questions of “general importance”, but then required that despite the “general importance” of the question, the court accept decisions of the Board that are wrong in law, even clearly wrong in law, but not patently unreasonable? The only way in which s. 83(1) can be given its explicitly articulated scope is if the Court of Appeal – and inferentially the Federal Court, Trial Division – is permitted to substitute its own opinion for that of the Board in respect of questions of general importance. This view accords with the observations of Iacobucci J. in Southam, supra, at para. 36, that a determination which has “the potential to apply widely to many cases” should be a factor in determining whether deference should be shown.
arguments.claim: Decisions such as Hilewitz, De Jong, and Pushpanathan suggest that questions of general importance require correctness standard review rather than deference.

arguments.quote: The respondent and intervener relied on Elezi v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FC 240, [2008] 1 F.C.R. 365 [Elezi] and, to a lesser extent, on Sanchez v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2009 FC 101, [2009] F.C.J No. 101, to argue that the RAD may take into account the probative value and credibility of evidence in order to counteract the requirements of subsection 110(4).
arguments.claim: The respondent and intervener argue that the RAD may consider the probative value and credibility of evidence to counteract subsection 110(4) requirements.

arguments.quote: As noted above, the judge refused to transpose the implicit admissibility criteria identified by the Court of Appeal regarding paragraph 113(a) to the context of subsection 110(4). Relying on the fact that questions relating to credibility, relevance, newness and materiality arise implicitly from the purpose of paragraph 113(a), as Justice Sharlow herself declared, the judge was of the opinion that the different role and status of the RAD as compared to that of a PRRA officer called for a distinctive analysis.
arguments.claim: The judge refused to apply the implicit admissibility criteria from paragraph 113(a) to subsection 110(4), citing the different role and status of the RAD compared to a PRRA officer.

arguments.quote: It is true that the French iteration of subsection 110(4) differs slightly from paragraph 113(a), insofar as it does not state “that the applicant could not reasonably have been expected…to have presented” (« qu’il n’était pas raisonnable … de s’attendre à ce qu’il les ait présentés »), but rather “that the person could not reasonably …have presented” (« qu’elle n’aurait pas normalement présentés »). I would agree with the judge that this distinction is not particularly telling, nor is it sufficient, in and of itself, to set aside past jurisprudence that has developed with regard to paragraph 113(a).
arguments.claim: The French version of subsection 110(4) differs slightly from paragraph 113(a) but this difference is not sufficient to set aside past jurisprudence related to paragraph 113(a).

arguments.quote: In addition, no great inference may be drawn from the absence of the word “new” in the English version of subsection 110(4). Not only is the word “new” (« nouveau ») nowhere to be found in the French version of paragraph 113(a), but it is furthermore self-evident that evidence that arose after the rejection of the refugee protection claim will necessarily be new.
arguments.claim: No significant inference can be drawn from the absence of the word 'new' in the English version of subsection 110(4) because the French version of paragraph 113(a) also lacks the word 'new' and evidence arising after rejection is necessarily new.

arguments.quote: The fact that the RAD is a quasi-judicial administrative tribunal, as opposed to the PRRA officer, who is an employee of the Minister, acting within his or her employer’s discretion, must obviously be taken into consideration. The same applies to the fact that the RAD has an appellate function and has the authority to set aside the RPD’s decision and substitute that which should have been made, while the PRRA officer must show deference and does not sit in appeal of the RPD’s decision and his or her only mission is to assess any new pre-removal risk. These distinctions are not determinative of the admissibility of new evidence, however, and I note that the trial judge did not specify how the distinctive role and status of the RAD and the PRRA officer should affect the criteria for admitting evidence or how it would allow for the negation of the presumption to which I referred above.
arguments.claim: The RAD's status as a quasi-judicial administrative tribunal with appellate function differs from the PRRA officer's role but these distinctions do not determine the admissibility of new evidence.

arguments.quote: In fact, the criteria used in Raza are consistent with the tests generally adopted by courts and administrative bodies, and are essentially designed to preserve the integrity of the judicial process: see Public School Boards’ Assn. of Alberta v. Alberta (Attorney General), 2000 SCC 2 at para 10, [2000] 1 S.C.R. 44. Although they were established by the Supreme Court in the context of a criminal proceeding (see Palmer v. The Queen, [1980] 1 S.C.R. 759 at p. 775, 106 D.L.R. (3d) 212 [Palmer]), the criteria of newness, relevance, credibility and materiality were subsequently applied in civil matters (J.T.I MacDonald Corp. v. Canada (Attorney General), 2004 CanLII 30110 at para. 3, [2004] J.Q. no 9409 (C.A.Q.), in disciplinary law (Morin v. Regional Administration Unit #3 (P.E.I.), 2002 PESCAD 9 at para. 140, 213 D.L.R. (4th) 17 (P.E.I.C.A.), in aboriginal law (Chippewas of Nawash First Nation v. Canada (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans), 2002 FCA 22 at para. 20, [2002] F.C.J No. 146) and in a number of other areas (see Donald J.M. Brown, Civil Appeals, Carswell, Toronto, 2015, pp. 10-16 to 10-18).
arguments.claim: The criteria used in Raza for admitting new evidence—newness, relevance, credibility, and materiality—are consistent with tests generally adopted by courts and administrative bodies to preserve judicial integrity.

arguments.quote: Indeed, Rules 3(3)(g)(iii) and 5(2)(d)(ii) of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules, S.O.R./2012-257 implicitly allude to this by providing that both the appellant’s memorandum and memorandum in reply must include full and detailed submissions regarding how any documentary evidence the appellant wishes to rely on not only meets the requirements of subsection 110(4), but also how that evidence relates to the appellant (« la façon dont ils sont liés à l’appelant »).
arguments.claim: Rules 3(3)(g)(iii) and 5(2)(d)(ii) of the Refugee Appeal Division Rules require appellants to show how documentary evidence meets subsection 110(4) and relates to the appellant.

arguments.quote: This is what the RAD aptly highlighted at paragraph 20 of its reasons: On this topic, it should be noted that the fact that evidence corroborates facts, contradicts RPD findings or clarifies evidence before the RPD does not make it “new evidence” within the meaning of subsection 110(4) of the Act. If that were the case, refugee protection claimants could split their evidence and present evidence before the RAD at the appeal stage that could have been presented at the start, before the RPD.
arguments.claim: Evidence that corroborates facts, contradicts RPD findings, or clarifies evidence before the RPD does not constitute 'new evidence' under subsection 110(4).

arguments.quote: However, it is her opinion that a strict interpretation of subsection 110(4) would limit an applicant’s access to a “full fact-based appeal,” which would go against the wishes expressed by Jason Kenney, former Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, in a statement made in the House on March 6, 2012 (House of Commons Debates, 41st Parl., 1st Sess., No. 90 (March 6, 2012) at p. 5874).
arguments.claim: A strict interpretation of subsection 110(4) would limit an applicant’s access to a full fact-based appeal, contrary to the wishes expressed by the former Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.

arguments.quote: In this regard, I support the argument of the appellant and his analysis of the circumstances in which the Minister made his statement.
arguments.claim: The Minister's statement supports differentiating the appeal from the narrower scope of judicial review and does not override subsection 110(4).

arguments.quote: The judge also based the decision on the reduced timeframes within which claimants must submit their documents to support the flexible interpretation of the admissibility criteria she considered in her decision.
arguments.claim: Reduced timeframes for submitting documents justify a flexible interpretation of the admissibility criteria to allow more evidence on appeal.

arguments.quote: Inversely, the desire to counter the abuses that could occur under the regime applicable before the BRRA and the Protecting Canada’s Immigration System Act, S.C. 2012, c. 17 came into force should not be invoked to restrict new evidence that those finding themselves with valid reason before the RAD should seek to file.
arguments.claim: The desire to counter abuses under previous regimes should not restrict new evidence that valid appellants seek to file before the RAD.

arguments.quote: Undoubtedly, Parliament intended to ensure the integrity of the immigration system by more effectively countering individuals who try to abuse it. To do so, Parliament took a certain number of measures, such as the creation of the RAD, and set out clear rules of evidence and procedure to ensure its appropriate functioning. These rules must be respected, and it must be presumed that the explicit choices that were made match the objective pursued.
arguments.claim: Parliament intended to ensure the integrity of the immigration system by setting clear rules of evidence and procedure for the RAD, which must be respected.

arguments.quote: Finally, the intervener stated that the RAD should take its inspiration from the values enshrined in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, Part I of the Constitution Act, 1982, being Schedule B to the Canada Act, 1982 (UK), c. 11 [Charter] when it rules on the admissibility of new evidence. Based on paragraph 3(3)(d) of the IRPA, further to which the Act is to be construed and applied in a manner that ensures that decisions taken under this Act are consistent with the Charter, as well as the decisions rendered by the Supreme Court in Doré v. Barreau du Québec, 2012 SCC 12, [2012] 1 S.C.R. 395 [Doré] and Loyola High School v. Quebec (Attorney General), 2015 SCC 12, [2015] 1 S.C.R. 613 [Loyola], counsel for the intervener claimed that the RAD had to go beyond the requirements set out in subsection 110(4) and was obligated to proceed with a proportionality analysis between the seriousness of the violation of the Charter right and the statutory objectives.
arguments.claim: The RAD should apply a proportionality analysis under the Charter when ruling on admissibility of new evidence, going beyond subsection 110(4) requirements.

arguments.quote: The following is how counsel described the test they propose (in paragraph 34 of their factum): (a) If the evidence is capable of credibly proving relevant circumstances that arose after the RPD’s decision, then the evidence must be considered. (b) If the evidence is only capable of credibly proving relevant circumstances that arose prior to the RPD’s decision, then the RAD should consider if the appellant established either (i) that the evidence was not reasonably available or (ii) that she could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented it, at the time of the RPD decision. In this assessment, the RAD should recall that « in order for there to be a ‘full fact-based appeal’ before the RAD, the criteria for the admissibility of evidence must be sufficiently flexible to ensure it can occur » [Singh v. Canada (MCI), 2014 FC 1022 at para. 55, per Gagné J.]. If the appellant is able to establish either condition, then the evidence must be admitted. (c) If the appellant is unable to satisfy either condition, then the RAD should consider whether the evidence raises a prima facie case of risk and, if admitted, could allow the RAD to come to a different conclusion on a central aspect of the claim than that of the RPD. If it does, then the RAD must conduct a proportionality exercise in which it balances the severity of the interference that exclusion would cause to the appellant’s Charter rights with the statutory objectives underlying s. 110(4).
arguments.claim: The proposed test requires admitting evidence if it credibly proves relevant circumstances arising after the RPD decision, or if prior circumstances evidence was not reasonably available or could not reasonably have been presented, and if not, admitting evidence that raises a prima facie risk and could change the RAD's conclusion, followed by a proportionality exercise balancing Charter rights and statutory objectives.

arguments.quote: Based on this approach, counsel for the intervener claim that the values protected by section 7 of the Charter must enter into the interpretation and application of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA and even lead to the admissibility of new evidence that does not meet the explicit requirements of this provision.
arguments.claim: Section 7 Charter values must influence interpretation and application of subsection 110(4) IRPA, leading to admitting new evidence even if it does not meet explicit requirements.

arguments.quote: The intervenor argued that excluding credible evidence could result in an appeal being dismissed and consequently in the removal of the foreign national “as soon as possible”, because the conditional removal order comes into force 15 days after notification that the claim is rejected (IRPA, s. 49(2)c)).
arguments.claim: Excluding credible evidence could lead to removal of the foreign national soon after claim rejection, affecting life, liberty, and security rights.

arguments.quote: Second, the intervenor did not convince me that the RAD’s decision not to admit new evidence would engage the principles of fundamental justice.
arguments.claim: The RAD’s decision not to admit new evidence engages the principles of fundamental justice.

arguments.quote: Furthermore, the respondent contends that he only learned in June 2013 that his lawyer before the RPD had received a copy of that document in February 2013.
arguments.claim: The respondent contends he only learned in June 2013 that his lawyer had received the Diploma in February 2013.
arguments.outcome_note: Accepted the timing claim but not that it relieves responsibility.

arguments.quote: In this case, the judge determined that it was unreasonable for the RAD to expect the applicant to know of the complaints procedure before the Barreau du Québec, much less be willing to attack the competence and ethics of his former counsel.
arguments.claim: The judge found it unreasonable to expect the applicant to know of the complaints procedure or to attack his former counsel’s competence and ethics.
arguments.outcome_note: No precedent cited and ignores applicant was represented by experienced counsel.

arguments.quote: Lastly, the judge invoked the possibility that inadmissibility of evidence could give rise to “serious issues of procedural equity” because a claimant who is deserving of a hearing could be refused one. In her opinion, such was the case here: “In the case at bar, the applicant was in fact denied a hearing because the 2002 school diploma was deemed inadmissible” (para. 53).
arguments.claim: The judge argued that inadmissibility of evidence could cause serious procedural equity issues by denying a deserving claimant a hearing.
arguments.outcome_note: The Court does not decide this issue here.

arguments.quote: It should be recalled that the RPD found that the respondent’s narrative was deficient in several respects: he contradicted himself about precisely when his father had had a heart attack; neither his allegations of torture nor his father’s purported medical condition are corroborated by the medical evidence; he presented as evidence fraudulent and altered documents; and he took no steps to obtain probative, acceptable documents with which to establish his identity.
arguments.claim: The RPD found the respondent’s narrative deficient due to contradictions about his father's heart attack timing, lack of corroboration of torture and medical conditions, presentation of fraudulent and altered documents, and failure to obtain probative identity documents.

holdings.quote: The matter before the Court is an appeal from a judgment of Justice Jocelyne Gagné of the Federal Court (the judge), which allowed the application for judicial review of Parminder Singh (the respondent) of a decision of the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada regarding his claim for refugee protection.
holdings.statement: The applicant is the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, appealing a Federal Court judgment that allowed the respondent Parminder Singh's judicial review application against a Refugee Appeal Division decision.

holdings.quote: The respondent’s refugee protection claim had previously been dismissed by the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), not only because he had failed to satisfactorily establish his identity, but because he was not credible and had an internal flight alternative available to him in India.
holdings.statement: The respondent Parminder Singh's refugee protection claim was dismissed by the Refugee Protection Division due to failure to establish identity, lack of credibility, and availability of an internal flight alternative in India.

holdings.quote: The appeal raises for the first time the issue as to how to interpret subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27 [IRPA], which governs admissible evidence before the RAD.
holdings.statement: The appeal concerns the interpretation of subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, which governs admissible evidence before the Refugee Appeal Division.

holdings.quote: This provision was enacted as part of the Balanced Refugee Reform Act, S.C. 2010, c. 8 [BRRA], the objective of which was to amend and implement unproclaimed provisions in the IRPA providing for the creation of the RAD.
holdings.statement: Subsection 110(4) was enacted as part of the Balanced Refugee Reform Act to implement provisions for the creation of the Refugee Appeal Division.

holdings.quote: At the end of her reasons, the judge certified the following two questions: 1. What standard of review should be applied by this Court when reviewing the Refugee Appeal Division’s interpretation of subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27? 2. In considering the role of a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment officer and that of the Refugee Appeal Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board sitting in appeal of a decision of the Refugee Protection Division, does the test set out in Raza v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2007 FCA 385, for the interpretation of paragraph 113(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, LC 2001, c 27, apply to its subsection 110(4)?
holdings.statement: The Federal Court judge certified two questions regarding the standard of review for the Refugee Appeal Division's interpretation of subsection 110(4) and the applicability of the Raza test to subsection 110(4).

holdings.quote: For the reasons that follow, I am of the view that the Minister’s submissions must be accepted and that the appeal must therefore be allowed.
holdings.statement: The Minister's submissions must be accepted and the appeal allowed.

holdings.quote: I. Background [5] The respondent is a citizen of India. He alleges to have been friends with one Bhupinder Singh when he was pursuing his studies, but that he only saw him occasionally following his graduation in 2002.
holdings.statement: The respondent is a citizen of India who alleges friendship with Bhupinder Singh during his studies, with occasional contact after graduation in 2002.

holdings.quote: Nonetheless, this individual apparently showed up at the respondent’s home in November 2012 to spend the night, before leaving for an unknown destination.
holdings.statement: Bhupinder Singh visited the respondent's home in November 2012 to spend the night before leaving for an unknown destination.

holdings.quote: Several days later, the respondent claims that the police arrested him in order to question him about Bhupinder Singh. He was purportedly held and tortured for three days before being released without conditions, when representatives from his village intervened on his behalf.
holdings.statement: The respondent claims police arrested and tortured him for three days to question him about Bhupinder Singh, then released him after village representatives intervened.

holdings.quote: Following this incident, he was apparently hospitalized for stomach pains. In support of his claims, he submitted a medical certificate to the RPD indicating that he had received treatment for injuries and vomiting, which contained a list of prescribed medications.
holdings.statement: The respondent was hospitalized for stomach pains and submitted a medical certificate with treatment details to the Refugee Protection Division.

holdings.quote: About two weeks after this first incident, the respondent contends that the police arrested him a second time and detained him for 24 hours in order to question him further about Bhupinder Singh, before he was released once again due to the intervention of representatives from his village.
holdings.statement: About two weeks later, the respondent alleges a second police arrest and 24-hour detention for further questioning about Bhupinder Singh, followed by release due to village intervention.

holdings.quote: After this second incident, the respondent alleges that his mother hired a smuggler to get him out of India. The respondent arrived in Canada on January 29, 2013, and claimed refugee protection at the port of entry.
holdings.statement: After the second incident, the respondent's mother hired a smuggler to get him out of India; he arrived in Canada on January 29, 2013, and claimed refugee protection at the port of entry.

holdings.quote: He handed over to the CBSA the driver’s licence and voter’s card the smuggler had obtained for him, as well as two school certificates issued in 2000 and 2002. The documents were seized, and the CBSA concluded after an analysis that the driver’s licence and voter’s card were probably forgeries.
holdings.statement: The respondent handed over a driver's licence, voter’s card, and two school certificates to CBSA; the driver's licence and voter’s card were deemed probably forged and seized.

holdings.quote: The respondent was initially detained due to the difficulty in establishing his identity, and was later released on condition that he report weekly to the CBSA’s offices.
holdings.statement: The respondent was initially detained due to identity issues and later released on condition of weekly reporting to CBSA.

holdings.quote: The hearing before the RPD was held on April 2, 2013, and the notice of that decision was issued on May 7, 2013.
holdings.statement: The Refugee Protection Division hearing was held on April 2, 2013, with decision issued May 7, 2013.

holdings.quote: IV. Analysis A. Standard of review [22] It is well-settled that the role of this Court when hearing an appeal of a judgment on an application for judicial review is to determine first, whether the Federal Court identified the appropriate standard of review and second, whether it applied that standard correctly: Agraira v. Canada (Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2013 SCC 36 at paras. 45-47, [2013] 2 S.C.R. 559;
holdings.statement: The Court's role on appeal of a judicial review application is to determine whether the Federal Court identified the appropriate standard of review and applied it correctly.

holdings.quote: In this instance, we are not confronted with a persistent discord that has existed for many years. The RAD was established in December 2012, and only began issuing decisions in 2013. There is therefore no urgent need to intervene, especially since the principles that will emerge from the jurisprudence of this Court and the Federal Court will necessarily provide a framework within which the RAD will be able to interpret subsection 110(4) of the IRPA. Thus, there is no need to depart from the general principle that an administrative tribunal is owed deference when it interprets its enabling statute; the early, tentative steps of the RAD and its differences of opinion as to the interpretation of certain statutory provisions do not affect the rule of law and are merely the inevitable consequence of choosing to entrust a specialized tribunal with the task of adjudicating disputes arising from the implementation of a new scheme.
holdings.statement: There is no urgent need to intervene in the RAD's interpretation of subsection 110(4) because the RAD is new and its early differences are inevitable and do not affect the rule of law.

holdings.quote: Yet the Supreme Court decided otherwise. In a recent decision, the highest court concluded that the presence of a certified question was not determinative and that the applicable standard of review for such questions is reasonableness: Kanthasamy v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 SCC 61 at para. 44, [2015] S.C.J. No. 61. In order to reach such a conclusion, the Court essentially relied on the fact that it is the judgment itself that is ultimately the subject of an appeal, and not merely the certified question.
holdings.statement: The Supreme Court decided that the presence of a certified question is not determinative and that the applicable standard of review for such questions is reasonableness.

holdings.quote: For all of these reasons, I therefore conclude that the judge correctly identified the standard of review to be applied to the application for judicial review that was before her. In other words, the RAD’s interpretation of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA was subject to review on the reasonableness standard, in accordance with the presumption that an administrative body’s interpretation of its home statute is owed deference by a reviewing court.
holdings.statement: The judge correctly identified the standard of review as reasonableness for the RAD’s interpretation of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, consistent with the presumption of deference to administrative bodies interpreting their home statute.

holdings.quote: I would hasten to add, as the judge did, that the present appeal does not turn on the role of the RAD and on the standard of review it should apply when ruling on decisions issued by the RPD, but solely on the factors the RAD must consider when assessing the admissibility of evidence that was not presented before the RPD.
holdings.statement: The present appeal focuses solely on the factors the RAD must consider when assessing the admissibility of evidence not presented before the RPD, not on the RAD's role or standard of review of RPD decisions.

holdings.quote: I would first note that Elezi was issued nine months before the Court of Appeal’s ruling in Raza, and is therefore no longer authoritative insofar as it departs from this later decision.
holdings.statement: Elezi is no longer authoritative to the extent it departs from the later Court of Appeal ruling in Raza.

holdings.quote: As a result, the assertion that one cannot reject credible evidence on the sole ground that it is “technically inadmissible” must be considered purely as an obiter.
holdings.statement: The assertion that credible evidence cannot be rejected solely because it is technically inadmissible is obiter in Elezi.

holdings.quote: The true crux of the issue here consists in determining whether the implied conditions of admissibility identified in the context of paragraph 113(a) by Justice Sharlow in Raza are also applicable to subsection 110(4).
holdings.statement: The key issue is whether the implied admissibility conditions identified in paragraph 113(a) by Justice Sharlow in Raza apply also to subsection 110(4).

holdings.quote: It must be assumed that Parliament’s decision to use near-identical wording did not happen by chance. Under a well-known rule of interpretation, it must be presumed that Parliament, when it uses the same wording as a provision that has already been interpreted by the courts, intends to rely on that interpretation: see Elmer A. Driedger, Construction of Statutes, 2nd ed., Toronto, Butterworths, 1983 at p. 125.
holdings.statement: It must be assumed that Parliament intended the same interpretation for subsection 110(4) as for paragraph 113(a) because of the near-identical wording.

holdings.quote: There is no doubt that the explicit conditions set out in subsection 110(4) have to be met. Accordingly, only the following evidence is admissible: • Evidence that arose after the rejection of the claim; • Evidence that was not reasonably available; or • Evidence that was reasonably available, but that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection.
holdings.statement: Only evidence that arose after the rejection of the claim, was not reasonably available, or could not reasonably have been expected to be presented at the time of rejection is admissible under subsection 110(4).

holdings.quote: These conditions appear to me to be inescapable and would leave no room for discretion on the part of the RAD. In the first place, the very wording of subsection 110(4) specifies that the person who is the subject of the appeal “may present only” (« ne peut présenter ») evidence that falls into one of these three categories, thereby excluding any other evidence. Second, one should not lose sight of the fact that this provision departs from the general principle according to which the RAD proceeds without a hearing, on the basis of the RPD’s record (s. 110(3)) and must for that reason be narrowly interpreted.
holdings.statement: The conditions in subsection 110(4) are inescapable and leave no room for discretion by the RAD to admit other evidence.

holdings.quote: Indeed, in my view it would be difficult to argue that the criteria set out by Justice Sharlow in Raza do not flow just as implicitly from subsection 110(4) as from paragraph 113(a).
holdings.statement: The criteria of newness, relevance, credibility, and materiality implicitly flow from subsection 110(4) as they do from paragraph 113(a).

holdings.quote: It is difficult to see, in particular, how the RAD could admit documentary evidence that was not credible. Indeed, paragraph 171(a.3) expressly provides that the RAD “may receive and base a decision on evidence that is adduced in the proceedings and considered credible or trustworthy in the circumstances.”
holdings.statement: The RAD cannot admit documentary evidence that is not credible, as paragraph 171(a.3) requires evidence to be credible or trustworthy in the circumstances.

holdings.quote: It is true that paragraph 110(6)(a) also introduces the notion of credibility for the purposes of determining whether a hearing should be held. In that regard, however, it is not the credibility of the evidence itself that must be weighed, but whether otherwise credible evidence “raises a serious issue” with respect to the general credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal. In other words, the fact that new evidence is intrinsically credible will not be sufficient to warrant holding a hearing before the RAD: this evidence would still be required to justify a reassessment of the overall credibility of the applicant and his or her narrative.
holdings.statement: For holding a hearing under paragraph 110(6)(a), the issue is whether credible evidence raises a serious issue about the appellant's overall credibility, not the intrinsic credibility of the new evidence itself.

holdings.quote: The same would apply to relevance. This is a basic condition for the admissibility of any piece of evidence, and it would be difficult to imagine the introduction of new evidence being somehow exempt from this criterion.
holdings.statement: Relevance is a basic condition for admissibility of any evidence, including new evidence under subsection 110(4).

holdings.quote: The newness criterion may appear somewhat redundant and does not really add to the explicit requirements of subsection 110(4).
holdings.statement: The newness criterion may be somewhat redundant and does not add much to the explicit requirements of subsection 110(4).

holdings.quote: As for the fourth implicit criterion identified by this Court in Raza, namely, the materiality of the evidence, there may be a need for some adaptations to be made. In the context of a PRRA, the requirement that new evidence be of such significance that it would have allowed the RPD to reach a different conclusion can be explained to the extent that the PRRA officer must show deference to a negative decision by the RPD and may only depart from that principle on the basis of different circumstances or a new risk. The RAD, on the other hand, has a much broader mandate and may intervene to correct any error of fact, of law, or of mixed fact and law. As a result, it may be that although the new evidence is not determinative in and of itself, it may have an impact on the RAD’s overall assessment of the RPD’s decision.
holdings.statement: The materiality criterion from Raza requires adaptation for the RAD context because the RAD has a broader mandate than the PRRA officer and may intervene to correct errors of fact or law.

holdings.quote: As a result, it may be that although the new evidence is not determinative in and of itself, it may have an impact on the RAD’s overall assessment of the RPD’s decision.
holdings.statement: Although new evidence may not be determinative by itself, it may impact the RAD's overall assessment of the RPD's decision.

holdings.quote: Under subsection 110(6) of the IRPA, a RAD hearing may be held, subject to three conditions associated with the existence of new documentary evidence. The principle whereby the RAD proceeds without holding a hearing, as set out in subsection 110(3), is subject to an exception only where the documentary evidence “(a) […] raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the person who is the subject of the appeal; (b) […] is central to the decision with respect to the refugee protection claim; and (c) […] if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.” These three conditions are unquestionably related to the materiality of the new documentary evidence that the RAD could be required to consider.
holdings.statement: Under subsection 110(6), a RAD hearing may be held only if new documentary evidence raises a serious issue about credibility, is central to the refugee protection claim decision, and if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the claim.

holdings.quote: If such is the case, as one would have reason to believe, it would be redundant to require materiality of evidence for it to be admissible as new evidence, to then subject the conduct of a hearing to the same criterion.
holdings.statement: It would be redundant to require materiality of evidence for admissibility and then again for holding a hearing under subsection 110(6).

holdings.quote: Subject to this necessary adaptation, it is my view that the implicit criteria identified in Raza are also applicable in the context of subsection 110(4). For the reasons set out above, I am not satisfied that the differing roles of the PRRA and the RAD, and the separate status of persons who perform these functions, are sufficient to set aside the presumption that Parliament intended to defer to the courts’ interpretation of a legislative text when it chose to repeat the same essential points in another provision. Not only are the requirements set out in Raza self-evident and widely applied by the courts in a range of legal contexts, but there are very good reasons why Parliament would favour a restrictive approach to the admissibility of new evidence on appeal.
holdings.statement: The implicit criteria identified in Raza are applicable to subsection 110(4) and the differing roles of PRRA and RAD do not justify setting aside the presumption that Parliament intended to defer to courts' interpretation of legislative text.

holdings.quote: As the Supreme Court noted in Palmer, a well-established judicial principle exists whereby the evidence and issues must be introduced exhaustively and dealt with at trial in criminal matters or at first instance in civil matters. As a case progresses, the issues in the matter must normally be further narrowed; the effect of introducing new evidence would be rather to expand the scope of the debate. In my opinion, this is exactly what subsection 110(4) of the Act seeks to prohibit.
holdings.statement: Parliament favors a restrictive approach to the admissibility of new evidence on appeal to preserve the integrity of the judicial process and avoid expanding the scope of debate at the appeal stage.

holdings.quote: At the risk of repeating myself, the basic rule is that the RAD “must proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the record of the proceedings of the Refugee Protection Division […]” (s. 110(3)). The new evidence must meet the admissibility criteria set out in subsection 110(4), and a new hearing can be held only if the new evidence fulfils the conditions set out in subsection 110(6).
holdings.statement: The RAD must proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the record of the proceedings of the Refugee Protection Division, and new evidence must meet the admissibility criteria set out in subsection 110(4) IRPA, with a new hearing only if conditions in subsection 110(6) are met.

holdings.quote: This legislative framework reflects Parliament’s clear wish to narrowly define the introduction of any new evidence.
holdings.statement: Parliament intended to narrowly define the introduction of any new evidence on appeal to the RAD.

holdings.quote: However, these considerations do not suffice to set aside the clear legislative intention to not authorize any new evidence on appeal other than in very specific and carefully defined circumstances.
holdings.statement: Although the IRPA amendments put pressure on claimants, these do not override the clear legislative intention to restrict new evidence on appeal to specific circumstances.

holdings.quote: The role of the RAD is not to provide the opportunity to complete a deficient record submitted before the RPD, but to allow for errors of fact, errors in law or mixed errors of fact and law to be corrected.
holdings.statement: The RAD's role is to correct errors of fact, law, or mixed errors, not to allow completion of a deficient record before the RPD.

holdings.quote: It is not the responsibility of the courts to rewrite such provisions when they are intelligible and unequivocal.
holdings.statement: It is not the courts' role to rewrite intelligible and unequivocal provisions of the IRPA regarding evidence admissibility.

holdings.quote: However, this thesis encounters at least two difficulties. First of all, it has not been established in this case that the values protected by section 7 of the Charter are affected by the RAD’s decision not to admit as new evidence the Diploma that the respondent wanted to adduce.
holdings.statement: This thesis encounters difficulties, including that it was not established that section 7 Charter values are affected by the RAD's decision not to admit the new evidence in this case.

holdings.quote: It is first noteworthy that the decision made by the RPD, and on appeal before the RAD, does not pertain to the respondent’s removal, but solely to whether he is genuinely a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection in accordance with sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA.
holdings.statement: The RAD's decision to exclude evidence concerns whether the respondent is a Convention refugee or person in need of protection, not removal.

holdings.quote: Nevertheless, the respondent in this case failed to establish his credibility; the RAD found that the RPD could reasonably conclude that the respondent’s credibility was seriously undermined, and that that conclusion would be valid even if the Diploma were admitted in evidence.
holdings.statement: The RAD found the respondent's credibility seriously undermined, and this conclusion would stand even if the new evidence were admitted.

holdings.quote: For reasons set out below, I am of the opinion that that conclusion falls within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes which are defensible in respect of the facts and the law, and consequently the respondent did not establish that his life, liberty or security would be in danger if he were returned to India.
holdings.statement: The respondent did not establish that his life, liberty, or security would be in danger if returned to India.

holdings.quote: It must be remembered that a foreign national claiming status as a refugee or a person in need of protection benefits from an extensive, multi-stage process that enables him to assert his claims before several levels of independent and impartial quasi-judicial tribunals and administrative decision-makers, and that he can apply for judicial review of those decisions to the Federal Court.
holdings.statement: A foreign national claiming refugee status benefits from a multi-stage process with several levels of independent tribunals and judicial review.

holdings.quote: While the right of appeal has not been recognized as a principle of fundamental justice (see Medovarski v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2005 SCC 51 at para. 47, [2005] 2 S.C.R. 539; Chiarelli v. Canada (Minister of Employment and Immigration), [1992] 1 S.C.R. 711 at pp. 741-742, 90 D.L.R. (4th) 289), Parliament decided to enhance the former regime and to implement the provisions of the IRPA establishing the RAD. The legislator could have provided only for an appeal on the record without a hearing, but elected to open the door to the submission of new evidence and hearings in carefully limited circumstances.
holdings.statement: Parliament enhanced the former regime by establishing the RAD, allowing submission of new evidence and hearings in limited circumstances.

holdings.quote: I fail to see how enhancing a system already broadly respectful of the international and constitutional obligations to which Parliament and the government are subject could jeopardize that same system, especially since the criteria used in respect of admissibility of new evidence are essentially similar to those normally used in judicial and quasi-judicial proceedings on appeal, in both civil and criminal matters.
holdings.statement: The criteria for admissibility of new evidence before the RAD are similar to those used in judicial and quasi-judicial appeals in civil and criminal matters.

holdings.quote: That said, I have not been convinced that the exclusion of the Diploma by the RAD is contrary to the principles of fundamental justice, even assuming that the exclusion of that evidence affects the respondent’s right to life, liberty and security.
holdings.statement: Excluding the Diploma by the RAD is not contrary to the principles of fundamental justice, even assuming it affects the respondent’s rights.

holdings.quote: A close reading of Doré shows that an administrative decision-maker’s obligation to enforce Charter values arises only if it is exercising statutory discretion: Doré, para. 55; Loyola, para. 35; R v. Clarke, 2014 SCC 28 at para. 16, [2014] 1 S.C.R. 612.
holdings.statement: An administrative decision-maker’s obligation to enforce Charter values arises only if exercising statutory discretion, per Doré and related cases.

holdings.quote: When legislation or regulations are clear and unambiguous, it is not up to the courts to rewrite them on the pretext of ensuring conformity with Charter values (Najafi v. Canada (Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness), 2014 FCA 262 at para. 107, [2015] 4 F.C.R. 162; Febles v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 SCC 68 at para. 67, [2014] 3 S.C.R. 431). Except under exceptional circumstances, the courts only have the authority to declare invalid legislation that is unconstitutional, and only if the issue is explicitly raised and the Attorney General has been notified. It is up to Parliament to amend legislation that has been declared unconstitutional so as to ensure compliance with the fundamental law of the land.
holdings.statement: Courts do not rewrite clear legislation to ensure conformity with Charter values; only Parliament can amend unconstitutional legislation.

holdings.quote: However, subsection 110(4) is not written in an ambiguous manner and does not grant any discretion to the RAD.
holdings.statement: Subsection 110(4) IRPA is clear and unambiguous and does not grant discretion to the RAD regarding admissibility of fresh evidence.

holdings.quote: As mentioned above (see paras. 34, 35 and 38 above), the admissibility of fresh evidence before the RAD is subject to strict criteria and neither the wording of the subsection nor the broader framework of the section it falls under could give the impression that Parliament intended to grant the RAD the discretion to disregard the conditions carefully set out therein.
holdings.statement: The admissibility of fresh evidence before the RAD is subject to strict criteria set by Parliament, not discretionary.

holdings.quote: Otherwise, this would mean ignoring the conditions set out at subsection 110(4) and then delving into a balancing exercise between Charter values and the objectives sought by Parliament. In the absence of a direct challenge to this legislation, it should be given effect and the RAD has no choice but to comply with its requirements.
holdings.statement: Ignoring subsection 110(4) conditions to balance Charter values and parliamentary objectives is not appropriate without a direct challenge to the legislation.

holdings.quote: In conclusion, I am of the view that there is no valid reason not to apply, for the most part, the implicit criteria established by this Court in Raza to subsection 110(4) of the IRPA. The wording of that provision is almost identical to the wording of paragraph 113(a), and the context in which it was adopted as well as the underlying judicial policy considerations support an identical approach despite the fact that they apply to separate proceedings and different decision-makers.
holdings.statement: The implicit criteria from Raza apply to subsection 110(4) IRPA as the wording and context are almost identical.

holdings.quote: In any case, the issue seems rather academic to me, to the extent that the implicit criteria from Raza do not truly add to the wording of subsection 110(4) but are necessarily implied. Except for the materiality of evidence, which does not lend itself to the same analysis in an appeal and which subsection 110(6) already considers in determining whether a new hearing should be held, it is not necessary to interpret subsection 110(4) and paragraph 113(a) differently.
holdings.statement: The implicit criteria from Raza do not add to subsection 110(4) except for materiality of evidence, which subsection 110(6) already considers.

holdings.quote: It goes without saying that the RAD always has the freedom to apply the conditions of subsection 110(4) with more or less flexibility depending on the circumstances of the case.
holdings.statement: The RAD has discretion to apply subsection 110(4) conditions with flexibility depending on case circumstances.

holdings.quote: Thus, it is my opinion that the RAD did not err in using “mutatis mutandis” the implicit criteria from Raza to interpret subsection 110(4); this interpretation seems not only reasonable but also correct.
holdings.statement: The RAD did not err in using the implicit criteria from Raza to interpret subsection 110(4); this interpretation is reasonable and correct.

holdings.quote: Furthermore, the RAD could reasonably find that the Diploma was inadmissible because it could not be considered fresh evidence.
holdings.statement: The RAD reasonably found the Diploma inadmissible as it was not fresh evidence.

holdings.quote: The RAD essentially based its finding on the fact that the respondent had access to the Diploma at the time of his hearing before the RPD on April 2, 2013, since the CBSA had sent a copy of it to his counsel and he could have obtained a copy from the CBSA and submitted it himself as evidence to the RPD.
holdings.statement: The RAD based its finding on the respondent having access to the Diploma at the RPD hearing time, as the CBSA sent a copy to his counsel.

holdings.quote: It is true that the immigration officer apparently did not submit the Diploma to the RPD, as he should have under subsection 3(5) of the RPD Rules.
holdings.statement: The immigration officer failed to submit the Diploma to the RPD as required by subsection 3(5) of the RPD Rules.

holdings.quote: However, that claim by itself is not enough to relieve the respondent of any responsibility.
holdings.statement: The respondent’s claim is insufficient to relieve him of responsibility for his counsel’s actions.

holdings.quote: Indeed, the Federal Court adopted a protocol in March 2014 outlining the procedure when a party wishes to make such an allegation, and in particular setting out the obligation to send a notice to counsel who is the subject of the allegations that are to be made against him or her and invite him or her to provide a response that could be submitted to the Court (Procedural Protocol Re: Allegations Against Counsel or Other Authorized Representative in Citizenship, Immigration and Protected Person Cases before the Federal Court (March 7, 2014), on line: Federal Court of Canada <http://www.fct-cf.gc.ca>).
holdings.statement: Federal Court protocol requires notice to counsel and opportunity to respond when allegations against counsel are made.

holdings.quote: In short, the RAD could reasonably conclude in the circumstances that the Diploma did not constitute new evidence. This piece of evidence is not new; it was accessible to the respondent, and his lawyer had received a copy from the CBSA.
holdings.statement: The RAD reasonably concluded the Diploma was not new evidence as it was accessible and counsel had received a copy from the CBSA.

holdings.quote: Since the respondent had not raised the issue of his lawyer’s incompetence nor lodged any complaint against her with the appropriate authorities, the RAD had no choice but to reject this evidence in accordance with subsection 110(4) of the IRPA.
holdings.statement: Since the respondent did not raise counsel incompetence or lodge complaints, the RAD had to reject the evidence under subsection 110(4) IRPA.

holdings.quote: However, as mentioned above, holding a hearing is not automatic simply because new evidence is admitted before the RAD.
holdings.statement: Holding a hearing is not automatic simply because new evidence is admitted before the RAD.

holdings.quote: This new evidence must still meet the three criteria set out in subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.
holdings.statement: New evidence must meet the three criteria set out in subsection 110(6) of the IRPA to be considered by the RAD.

holdings.quote: In this case, there was not even an attempt to show how the Diploma was determinative in establishing the respondent’s credibility and how it would make up for the various shortcomings that the RPD identified in his testimony and that were confirmed by the RAD.
holdings.statement: There was no attempt to show how the Diploma was determinative in establishing the respondent’s credibility or how it would compensate for the shortcomings identified by the RPD and confirmed by the RAD.

holdings.quote: In light of all these factors, it is far from a given that the Diploma would be essential in deciding the respondent’s refugee protection claim and would warrant allowing this claim.
holdings.statement: Given the deficiencies in the respondent’s narrative and evidence, it is not clear that the Diploma would be essential in deciding the refugee protection claim or justify allowing the claim.

holdings.quote: Consequently, it cannot be assumed that admitting this document into evidence would have led to a hearing or that its rejection undermined procedural fairness.
holdings.statement: It cannot be assumed that admitting the document into evidence would have led to a hearing or that its rejection undermined procedural fairness.

holdings.quote: Nor can one invoke the possibility that a hearing might have resulted from the admission into evidence of the Diploma to argue for a flexible interpretation of subsection 110(4): not only does holding a hearing in the present case seem highly theoretical, but the admissibility of a piece of evidence cannot be assessed by taking account of the consequences that could result for the purposes of applying subsection 110(6).
holdings.statement: The possibility that a hearing might have resulted from the admission of the Diploma cannot be used to argue for a flexible interpretation of subsection 110(4).

holdings.quote: V. Conclusion [73] For all the above reasons, I am of the opinion that the appeal should be allowed, that the Federal Court judgment should be set aside and that the RAD decision should be confirmed.
holdings.statement: The appeal should be allowed, the Federal Court judgment set aside, and the RAD decision confirmed.

holdings.quote: Accordingly, the respondent is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection within the meaning of sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA.
holdings.statement: The respondent is not a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection within the meaning of sections 96 and 97 of the IRPA.

holdings.quote: Answer: The RAD’s interpretation of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA must be reviewed in light of the reasonableness standard, in accordance with the presumption that an administrative agency’s interpretation of its home statute should be shown deference by the reviewing court. 2.
holdings.statement: The RAD’s interpretation of subsection 110(4) of the IRPA must be reviewed on a reasonableness standard, with deference to the administrative agency’s interpretation of its home statute.

holdings.quote: Answer: To determine the admissibility of evidence under subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, the RAD must always ensure compliance with the explicit requirements set out in this provision.
holdings.statement: To determine admissibility of evidence under subsection 110(4) of the IRPA, the RAD must ensure compliance with the explicit requirements of that provision.

holdings.quote: It was also reasonable for the RAD to be guided, subject to the necessary adaptations, by the considerations made by this Court in Raza.
holdings.statement: It was reasonable for the RAD to be guided, with necessary adaptations, by the considerations in Raza v Canada for interpreting subsection 110(4).

holdings.quote: However, the requirement concerning the materiality of the new evidence must be assessed in the context of subsection 110(6), for the sole purpose of determining whether the RAD may hold a hearing.
holdings.statement: The requirement concerning materiality of new evidence must be assessed in the context of subsection 110(6) solely to determine whether the RAD may hold a hearing.

rebuttals.quote: With respect, I am not persuaded by this argument.
rebuttals.court_answer: I am not persuaded by the argument that the judge erred in selecting the reasonableness standard.

rebuttals.quote: It should be noted that Wilson is an “unusual” case, to use the expression employed by Justice Stratas, in that the question as to whether the Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. L-2 permits dismissals on a without cause basis has been one of “persistent” discord, to the extent that the answer to this question has largely depended on the identity of the adjudicator.
rebuttals.court_answer: Wilson is an unusual case involving persistent discord dependent on the adjudicator's identity, unlike the present case.

rebuttals.quote: Furthermore, adjudicators are not bound by the decisions of their colleagues and operate independently rather than within an institution such as an administrative tribunal, which decidedly does not favour the emergence of a consensus or a consistent interpretation.
rebuttals.court_answer: Adjudicators operate independently and are not bound by colleagues' decisions, which does not favour consensus or consistent interpretation.

rebuttals.quote: With respect, I am unable to agree with this interpretation.
rebuttals.court_answer: I disagree with the interpretation that the RAD may consider probative value and credibility to override subsection 110(4).

rebuttals.quote: For the reasons that follow, I cannot subscribe to this view.
rebuttals.court_answer: I cannot agree with the judge's view that the RAD's different role requires a distinctive analysis from that applied to paragraph 113(a).

rebuttals.quote: This statement alone is insufficient to substantiate the theory that criteria explicitly set out at subsection 110(4) can be set aside. It is at best ambiguous, and could be simply construed as differentiating the appeal from the much narrower scope of a judicial review.
rebuttals.court_answer: The Minister's statement about a fact-based appeal is ambiguous and insufficient to set aside the explicit criteria in subsection 110(4).

rebuttals.quote: With respect, I cannot agree with this argument. It is true that, in Doré, the Supreme Court stated that it was of the opinion that an administrative decision-maker must weigh the values set out in the Charter and the statutory objectives in the exercise of his or her discretionary power. In the context of a judicial review, the Court must determine whether the decision under review is the result of a proportionate balancing of the rights and values protected by the Charter, a process that bears some resemblance to the framework of analysis established in R. v. Oakes, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 103, 26 D.L.R. (4th) 200 when the very validity of a legislative text is challenged.
